source.title: Control theory of stochastic distributed parameter systems: recent progress and open problems

accepted.question_text: For the controlled stochastic hyperbolic equation on a bounded domain G with state (y, y_t), drift control f, diffusion control g, and boundary control h, the paper proves that exact controllability fails even when all three controls are available. The open question is whether weaker target notions—null controllability or approximate controllability—still hold for this stochastic hyperbolic system, preferably with fewer controls than the original three-control setup, and how to prove the required observability estimate for the adjoint equation when the terms Z and O^Z do not appear on the observed right-hand side.

evidence.quote: Consider the following controlled stochastic hyperbolic equation: ... where the initial data (y0,y1) ... and f,g ... and h ... are three controls.

(1) Null and approximate controllability of stochastic hyperbolic equations. We have shown that the system (2.1) is not exactly controllable for any T > 0 and Γ0 ⊊ Γ. It is natural to ask whether it is null/approximately controllable. Of course, for these problems, fewer controls should be employed. The difficulty to do that lies in proving suitable observability estimate of equation (2.3), in which Z and O^Z do not appear in the right-hand side.

accepted.question_text: Consider the refined stochastic wave-like control system in which dy = ȳ dt + (a4 y + f) dW in Q, d ȳ - Σ_{j,k}(a_jk y_{x_j})_{x_k} dt = (a1·∇y + a2 y + a5 g) dt + (a3 y + g) dW in Q, y = χ_{Γ0} h on the boundary, and the controls are f, g, and h. Exact controllability is known for this model when the diffusion control g belongs to L²_F(0,T;H^{-1}(G)). The open question is whether exact controllability still holds when g is required only to lie in L²_F(0,T;L²(G)), equivalently whether one can prove the corresponding adjoint observability estimate using the boundary observation ∂z/∂ν on Γ0 together with the interior terms a5 z + Z and O^Z in L²(G).
accepted.context_brief: regularity of controls in exact controllability

evidence.quote: Motivated by this, we consider the following refined version of controlled stochastic hyperbolic equation: ... Here (y0, ȳ0) ... and f ∈ L²_F(0,T;L²(G)), g ∈ L²_F(0,T;H^{-1}(G)), and h ∈ L²_F(0,T;L²(Γ0)) are controls.

(2) Exact controllability for stochastic wave-like equations with more regular controls. Is the system (2.2) exactly controllable when g ∈ L²_F(0,T;L²(G))? The desired controllability is equivalent to the following observability estimate: ... But one cannot mimic the method in [37] to prove (4.1).

accepted.question_text: For stochastic parabolic equations viewed as stochastic distributed parameter systems, can null controllability or approximate controllability be obtained with only one control rather than two, beyond the special cases already known?

evidence.quote: (3) Null/approximate controllability for stochastic parabolic equations with one control. One needs two controls to get the null/approximate controllability for stochastic parabolic equations (e.g., [45]). We believe that one control is enough. However, except for some special cases (e.g., [23, 26]), we have no idea on how to prove that.

accepted.question_text: For stochastic parabolic equations, and more generally for stochastic distributed parameter systems, can one derive quantitative estimates for the control cost of approximate controllability, analogous to the known deterministic results for heat equations?

evidence.quote: (4) The cost for the approximate controllability for SDPSs. It is shown in [45] that stochastic parabolic equations are approximately controllable. But it does not give any estimate for the cost of the control. Can one generalize the results in [10] to stochastic parabolic equations? Furthermore, it deserves to study the cost of the approximate controllability for general SDPSs.

accepted.question_text: For semilinear stochastic distributed parameter systems, especially stochastic parabolic and stochastic hyperbolic equations, can one prove controllability results analogous to those known for deterministic semilinear distributed parameter systems, including cases where the nonlinearity grows more slowly than s log(s)^(3/2), and can one identify further classes of nonlinear terms for which controllability still holds?

evidence.quote: (5) Controllability for semilinear SDPSs. In [9], based on sharp estimates on the dependence of controls for the underlying linear equation perturbed by a potential and fixed point arguments, it was proved that semilinear parabolic and hyperbolic equations are null controllable with nonlinearities that grow slower than s log(s)^{3/2}. Whether such results can be obtained for semilinear stochastic parabolic/hyperbolic equations is open. On the other hand, for nonlinearities growing at infinity as s log(s)^p with p > 2, one cannot get the null controllability due to the blow-up of solutions. However, this does not exclude controllability for some particular classes of nonlinear terms (e.g., [7]). More generally, there are lots of interesting results for controllability of semilinear distributed parameter systems (e.g., [6]). So a systematic study of controllability problems for semilinear SDPSs deserves attention.

accepted.question_text: Can one develop a substantially stronger stabilization theory for stochastic distributed parameter systems, in particular proving stabilization results for stochastic hyperbolic equations with localized damping?

evidence.quote: (6) Stabilization of SDPSs. Stabilization for distributed parameter control systems is a well-studied area. In recent years, some progresses were obtained for SDPSs (e.g., [1,4]). However, this problem is far from being well understood. For example, as far as we know, there is no result for the stabilization of stochastic hyperbolic equations with localized damping.

accepted.question_text: For optimal control problems of stochastic distributed parameter systems with endpoint constraints or state constraints, can one derive nontrivial Pontryagin-type maximum principles under genuinely general constraints, for example by extending finite-codimensionality arguments or set-valued-analysis methods to the stochastic setting in a satisfactory way?

evidence.quote: (7) Optimal control problems for SDPSs with endpoint/state constraints. For some special constraints ... one can use the Ekeland variational principle to establish a Pontryagin-type maximum principle with nontrivial Lagrange multipliers. Nevertheless, for the general case, one does need some further conditions to obtain nontrivial results. ... There are some attempts to generalize this condition to the stochastic framework ... Another way is to use some tools from the set-valued analysis ... However, the existing results are still not satisfactory so far.

accepted.question_text: Let (3.7) denote the operator-valued backward stochastic evolution equation that currently has a unique relaxed transposition solution in the paper. Can one prove that this equation admits a unique transposition solution, not merely a relaxed transposition solution, in a substantially more general setting than the currently known very special case?
accepted.context_brief: transposition solution for second adjoint equation

evidence.quote: If (3.7) admits a transposition solution, then it has a relaxed transposition solution ... Until now, we have no idea how to prove the existence of a transposition solution to (3.7).

(8) Well-posedness of (3.7) in the sense of transposition solution. It would be quite important for some optimal control problems to prove that equation (3.7) admits a unique transposition solution. So far this is only done for a very special case (e.g., [33, Theorem 4.1]).

accepted.question_text: For optimal controls of stochastic distributed parameter systems, can one establish higher-order necessary conditions under weaker assumptions than those used in the existing literature, potentially by first proving the existence of a transposition solution to the second adjoint equation (3.7)?

evidence.quote: Q is used to get higher-order necessary conditions and to solve operator-valued backward stochastic Riccati equations ...

(9) Higher-order necessary conditions for optimal controls. Similar to calculus, in addition to the first-order necessary conditions (PMP), sometimes higher-order necessary conditions should be established to distinguish optimal controls from the candidates satisfying the first-order necessary conditions trivially. Some results in this direction for SDPSs can be found in [12, 13, 32]. However, these results were obtained only under very strong assumptions which should be relaxed. To this end, we believe one should first show the existence of a transposition solution to equation (3.7).

accepted.question_text: Outside the trivial situations listed in the survey—such as convex coercive costs on a closed convex control set or convex costs on a closed bounded convex control set—can one prove the existence of optimal controls for stochastic distributed parameter systems, for example via a verification theorem or by proving compactness of minimizing sequences in genuinely nontrivial settings?

evidence.quote: (10) Existence of optimal controls. We have discussed the necessary conditions for optimal controls without proving the existence of an optimal control, which is a very difficult problem. There are two general approaches available to study it. One is to prove the verification theorem, the other is to show that a minimizing sequence of controls is compact. Both methods have not been developed well for SDPSs. Except for some trivial cases ... there is no further result for that problem.

accepted.question_text: What is the precise relationship between Pontryagin's maximum principle and dynamic programming for stochastic distributed parameter systems, especially in the presence of possibly nonsmooth value functions and the derivative information needed to connect the two theories?

evidence.quote: (11) The relationship between PMP and dynamic programming for SDPSs. PMP and dynamic programming serve as two of the most important tools in solving optimal control problems. Both of them provide some necessary conditions for optimal controls. There should exist a basic link between them. This link is established for finite dimensional stochastic control systems (e.g., [47]). A possible relationship unavoidably involves the derivatives of the value functions, which could be nonsmooth in even very simple cases (e.g., [5]).

accepted.question_text: What general mathematical connection links controllability theory and optimal control theory for stochastic distributed parameter systems, especially for problems with endpoint state constraints, and how can the initial finite-codimensional exact controllability results be extended into a broader theory?

evidence.quote: (12) The connection between controllability and optimal control. The survey divides itself naturally into two parts—controllability and optimal control. There should be a close ...

relationship between these two topics. Some initial findings are given in [24], in which a new link between (finite-codimensional exact) controllability and optimal control problems for SDPSs with endpoint state constraints is presented. However, lots of things are to be done, which are by no means easy tasks.

accepted.question_text: Can one develop effective numerical methods for controllability and optimal control problems for stochastic distributed parameter systems, including numerical solution of the required adjoint equations and forward-backward stochastic evolution equations, beyond the limited existing results?

evidence.quote: (13) Numerics of the controllability and optimal control problems for SDPSs. By generalizing J.-L. Lions’ HUM ..., one can find the numerical solution to controllability problems of SDPSs by solving suitable adjoint equations numerically ... On the other hand, by Theorem 3.4, one can obtain an optimal control by solving suitable forward–backward stochastic evolution equation. Unfortunately, the numerical approximation of the equations mentioned above can be quite cumbersome. ... There are lots of things to be done.

accepted.question_text: In stochastic distributed parameter systems, uncertainty often makes control harder, but it can also create advantages. What mathematically useful benefits can be obtained from uncertainty, and how can those benefits be characterized and exploited systematically?

evidence.quote: (14) What can we benefit from the uncertainty? From Sections 2 and 3, we see that the uncertainty in SDPSs places many disadvantages for controlling the systems. Nevertheless, sometimes, surprisingly, it provides advantages (e.g., [34, 39]). What can we benefit from the uncertainty in SDPSs is far from being understood. We believe that the study for that problem will lead to new insights into uncertainty.
